[PAPER_0033, relevance_score=0.379] Our primary preregistered (https://osf.io/n36cu) hypothesis was that, during the training week, participants allocated to recall of positive AMs would experience a greater intraindividual increase in feelings of happiness from pre- to post-AM recollection, compared to individuals in the everyday activity condition. We further expected an intraindividual reduction of sadness in both the positive and everyday activity AM conditions, since everyday activity AMs may have a distracting effect. We hypothesized that this effect would strengthen over the course of the training week.

[PAPER_0034, relevance_score=0.332] We hypothesized that this effect would strengthen over the course of the training week. Our second preregistered hypothesis was that any benefits from the recollection of positive AMs would generalize to untrained memories, such that following study completion, participants in the positive AM condition would more readily retrieve other, untrained positive AMs that were more positive in valence, evoke more happiness and satisfaction, be more vivid, and more self-concordant relative to those in the everyday activity condition. We also evaluated the potential of this technique for reducing risk of depressive relapse.

[PAPER_0035, relevance_score=0.304] We also evaluated the potential of this technique for reducing risk of depressive relapse. To index acceptability and use, we hypothesized that individuals in the positive AM condition would demonstrate more frequent spontaneous (i.e., unprompted) use of the AM diary technique in the 2 weeks following training. We anticipated this effect would be stronger for those who experienced a greater improvement in feelings of happiness and a greater decrease in feelings of sadness during training (third preregistered hypothesis).

[PAPER_0036, relevance_score=0.323] To index potential effects on well-being, we explored whether those in the positive condition experienced an increase in well-being and a decrease in residual depressive symptoms from pre to post and to follow-up assessments, relative to the everyday activity condition (exploratory research question).

[PREREG_0004, relevance_score=0.382] In the present study we seek to train previously depressed individuals to counteract low or dipping mood in daily life through recollecting AMs of a pre-selected AM repository in a vivid and imagery-rich fashion using experience sampling methodology (ESM).

q4: Primary hypothesis (hypothesis 1): We hypothesise that participants in the positive self-affirming AM condition will experience a greater intraindividual increase in momentary happiness from pre to post AM recollection compared to individuals in the neutral condition during the practice period.

[PREREG_0006, relevance_score=0.398] Secondary hypothesis (hypothesis 2): We hypothesise that an independent set of 6 positive self-affirming AMs retrieved during the second laboratory session will on average be more positive in valence, more happy or satisfying upon recall, more vivid, and more self-concordant for individuals in the positive self-affirming AM condition (that is, that effects of training will generalise to positive memories that are not practiced) whereby controlling for the amount of practice with the diary.

[PREREG_0007, relevance_score=0.345] Feasibility (hypothesis 3): In the follow-up period, we expect that individuals in the positive AM condition will use the AM diary more often spontaneously. We will explore whether this effect is stronger for those who experience a greater improvement in momentary happiness and greater decrease in momentary sadness during the training period (i.e., a moderation effect).

[PREREG_0008, relevance_score=0.369] Exploratory: To determine the potential for a future relapse prevention study, we will explore whether the positive self-affirming AM group experiences an increase in wellbeing, relative to the neutral condition, from pre to post and follow-up assessments. We will also evaluate effects on residual depressive symptoms. We will further explore whether a potential increase in wellbeing and a decrease in depressive symptoms over the course of the study is mediated by the average experienced emotional benefits in happiness and sadness.

All analyses were preregistered and conducted in R, Version 4.1.0 (R Core Team, 2022), using RStudio, Version 2022.02.3 (RStudio Team, 2022). Group comparisons for descriptive statistics were made using χ2 tests and independent samples t tests for interval-scaled variables. Differences between observed frequencies were calculated using the χ2 goodness of fit test.

Time elapsed between the AM entries was modeled in days that had passed since the baseline session. We included a random intercept for days nested in participants and a random slope for the time elapsed between the AM entries (in days) in models to examine whether effects increased over the course of the study. We also corrected for nonindependence of the time series data by modeling a first-order autoregressive structure.

[PAPER_0077, relevance_score=0.373] Specifically, we predicted AM valence, happiness/satisfaction upon recall, AM vividness, and self-concordance by condition (positive vs. everyday activity) using multivariate linear regression with the "manova" function from the "stats" package (R Core Team, 2022). The number of AM entries across the 3-week period was a covariate.

Deviating from our preregistration, to evaluate feasibility, we predicted the number of spontaneous AM entries in the 2-week assessment period, per person by condition (positive vs.
